title: Abandoned Property and Tenant-Death Response Crew
one_liner: A per-event service that handles the legally dangerous moments landlords dread most, such as a tenant who vanishes leaving belongings or a tenant who dies alone, with statutory clocks, next-of-kin outreach and documented disposal.
customer: Property managers and small landlords, who pay per event ($400 to $1,500). Later customers are eldercare social workers, hospital discharge teams, medical examiners' offices and estate attorneys, who all need someone to close out a residence properly.
problem: A 400-unit manager deals with a handful of abandonments a year and one to three tenant deaths. Each event is handled ad hoc. Abandoned-property statutes vary by state, with notice periods, itemized inventory rules, value thresholds and sale-or-storage requirements. One mistake, such as tossing a bin or entering too early, creates conversion or wrongful-eviction liability. With a death, no one has authority to enter or dispose of belongings, the estate has no representative yet, next of kin are unknown or hostile, rent accrues, and the unit sits dark for months. Hoarding and biohazard situations make it worse. There is no standard vendor, so the maintenance supervisor is doing legal and emotional work no one trained him for.
solution: A regional response team with a state-specific statutory workflow. Step one is intake and legal-clock software, which starts the required notice dates, produces the notices, photo-inventory and valuation report and stores it as evidence. Step two is next-of-kin and estate-representative outreach, with sensitivity training for the caller. Step three is secure storage in a partner facility, then sale, donation or disposal exactly as the statute allows, with receipts. Step four is coordinating hoarding or biohazard remediation and the final walk-through for deposit accounting. A companion product is an e-signable lease addendum letting tenants (especially seniors) name an emergency contact and authorized person for post-death property disposition, in the states where that is permitted. That builds a pipeline of pre-authorized cases and makes each later event simple.
why_now: The number of renters aged 65+ living alone is growing fast, which means more deaths in rental units and more hoarding and welfare issues. Several states have recently added or modernized tenant-designated-contact and abandoned-property procedures, though rules remain patchy. Software-only proptech has ignored this because it is field work. Junk-removal and storage marketplaces have made the physical logistics cheap to subcontract.
revenue_model: $400 to $1,500 flat fee per abandonment or death event, plus pass-through storage and disposal cost at a 15 to 25% markup. Optional readiness subscription ($1 to $2 per unit per month) for PMs, covering the lease addendum, templates and priority response. Eldercare and estate-attorney referral relationships add a second channel.
non_obvious_insight: Ordinary landlords fear the eviction. Experienced managers fear the abandonment and the death, because the law in those cases punishes shortcuts, no procedure exists, and the loss (months of rent plus liability) is bigger than a normal eviction. Nobody sells the service because each case is small and the required knowledge is a stack of 50 state statutes. That fragmentation is the moat: once you have playbooks for a handful of states, competitors cannot copy them quickly.
first_30_days: Pick one state and read the abandoned-property and death-of-tenant statutes closely, ideally with a landlord-tenant attorney on a fixed-fee review. Build the notice, inventory and timeline templates. Sign three PMs (find them through the local NARPM or apartment association) to a pilot: 'call us on the next event, first one at cost'. Line up a junk-removal company, a storage unit partner and a biohazard remediation subcontractor. Publish a simple blog page and a landlord-association talk titled 'What to do when a tenant dies or disappears' to start inbound.

title: Vet Tech Apprenticeship Intermediary
one_liner: Registered-apprenticeship sponsorship as a service, letting clinics grow their own technicians through a paid pathway with wage support and retention contracts.
customer: Clinics and groups with 3 or more open assistant or tech roles, plus state workforce boards that fund apprenticeships.
problem: Figures from a trade opinion piece (directional only): about 2 techs per vet versus a 4:1 ideal, most techs leave within 4 years, techs average about $45K, program enrollment is down 43%, and only about 7,000 of 14,000 needed new techs sit for licensing exams each year. Clinics cannot release staff for classroom time, and on-the-job training is unstructured.
solution: We register and manage an apprenticeship program as sponsor of record. Each apprentice pairs with an accredited distance-learning tech program, an on-site mentor (trained by us), a competency logbook and a wage-step schedule with a retention agreement. We file paperwork for state and workforce-board funds and track progress toward the licensing exam.
why_now: There is a 2025-26 push at the federal and state level to expand apprenticeships and fund workforce pathways (verify state programs). A new supervised professional tier (Colorado's VPA) raises demand for skilled support staff, and clinics are desperate for retention tools.
revenue_model: $250-400 per apprentice per month, a $500 clinic setup fee, and a share of state grants. Multi-clinic groups pay for program licenses.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is discussed as 'not enough schools'. The real bottleneck is that employers cannot afford to release staff and have no retention hook. An apprenticeship converts an assistant already on payroll into a tech, with public money and a contract that keeps them.
first_30_days: Map which states permit apprenticeship or on-the-job routes to licensing and pick two. Get 3-5 clinics to commit 1-2 apprentices each. Partner with an accredited distance program. Begin state registration and charge a $500 setup fee to lock in clinics.

title: Own-Your-Office Buyer Groups for Practices
one_liner: Assemble dentists, clinics, law and accounting firms into buyer clubs that buy discounted vacant office buildings and split them into owner-occupied condos financed with SBA loans.
customer: Small professional practices renting 3,000-15,000 sf each (5-20 per building), plus special servicers and receivers who need a bulk exit for distressed office.
problem: National office vacancy is 17.8%, office CMBS delinquency 13.2%, $39B of office debt matures within 12 months and $289B by 2028 on about 14,000 properties. Sellers are forced, but institutional buyers price office as an income asset and few small buyers can act. Small practices keep paying roughly $33 asking rent with escalators and never see the building trade at a fraction of replacement cost.
solution: Pre-qualify 8-15 owner-users (financials and SBA 504/7(a) eligibility), find 40-150k sf Class B buildings from servicers at low per-sf bases, create a condo declaration and a single purchasing entity, close in bulk, then finance and deed units individually to practices (each occupying its own space). Keep the association-management and repositioning contract.
why_now: Servicers are actively seeking exits and most B/C buildings do not pencil for residential conversion, so owner-occupancy is the highest and best use. SBA programs finance owner-occupants at very high LTV, and high rates make a lease a large fixed cost relative to ownership.
revenue_model: 2-4% sponsor fee per unit sold, condo-ization margin or promote on unsold units, and recurring building/association management ($0.60-1.00 per sf per year) plus resale commissions.
non_obvious_insight: Investors value office on cash-flow multiples, while owner-users value it at the rent they would otherwise pay. At distressed bases the owner-user's willingness to pay can exceed the investor's bid, and no one is aggregating this fragmented demand against a forced-seller supply pool.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with cheap Class B office. Launch a landing page and outreach through dental, medical and CPA associations and SBA/CDC lenders. Collect 10 non-binding letters of intent from practices. Approach 2-3 servicer asset managers about bulk-sale listings. Charge a refundable $2,500 deposit for founding-member slots.

title: Real-Pixel Blink Fixer for Family Formals
one_liner: A Lightroom/Photoshop plugin that turns a 5-frame burst of the 30-person family formal into one frame where every set of eyes is open, using only real pixels from the burst and no generated faces.
customer: Solo and small-studio wedding photographers (roughly 100k in the US), paying $29-49/mo or about $2 per composite. Later extension: school, team, church and corporate group-portrait photographers.
problem: Family formals are the 20-40 minute block of the day that grandparents care about most. They are also mathematically hostile. If each person has their eyes closed about 8% of the time, a 30-person frame has under a 10% chance of everyone being open, before counting people who look away or squint. So the delivered frame is nearly always a compromise or a composite. Photographers either hand-swap heads in Photoshop (20-40 minutes per group, or $15-40 per image if outsourced), ship the frame with the blinker, or use generative fill. Generative fill invents a face, which is a betrayal when the face is a grandfather who won't be there in two years.
solution: Drop in the formals folder. The tool groups frames into bursts, aligns them (people shift between frames), scores each person's face for eyes open, smile, gaze and sharpness, picks the best patch per person, and blends with seam-aware masks. The output is a layered PSD so the photographer can override any face in one click. The pitch is a strict 'zero generative pixels' guarantee. A second mode is a shoot-time phone companion that says 'frame 3 has 2 blinkers, shoot one more' so bursts are captured with enough variety. The wedge is batch mode for formals only, not a full editor.
why_now: Google's Best Take (Pixel 8, 2023) taught consumers to expect a merged best-expression group photo. Photographers already pay monthly for AI culling and editing, so AI tooling is normal spend in this trade. Adobe's own face-swap route leans on generative fill, which many pros distrust for client faces. On-device face-landmark and eye-state models are now cheap and accurate enough to run locally on a laptop. Searches in Sept 2026 found only manual Photoshop tutorials for this, not a dedicated automated burst-composite product.
revenue_model: Subscription of $29/mo for solo shooters or $2 per composite credit with monthly bundles. Studio plans at $79/mo. Optional white-label API for gallery platforms (Pic-Time, ShootProof-type) later.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody outside the trade realizes that a truly 'perfect' 30-person frame almost never exists in a single exposure, so every delivered formal is quietly a fix or a compromise. The fix that matters is provenance: the people who print the formals at 16x20 are the elderly relatives, and they will notice an AI-invented face on Grandpa. 'Real pixels only' is the actual feature, not the face-swapping.
first_30_days: Build against Lightroom Classic/Photoshop with open-source face-landmark models. Ask 20 photographers in Facebook groups and r/WeddingPhotography to send 3 old formals bursts from past weddings (every working shooter has hundreds sitting in archives). Return composites in 24 hours with before/after slider pages. First 10 composites free, then $2 each via Stripe. Post the before/afters and blink-probability math in photographer communities. Goal is 30 paying studios and one gallery-platform partnership conversation by day 90.

title: Exposure Response Desk for Vibe-Coded Apps
one_liner: A fix-and-legal-decision service for founders whose AI-built apps leaked user data, delivering an RLS lockdown, an access-log check and a breach-notification memo.
customer: Non-technical founders and small businesses that shipped apps on Lovable, Bolt, Replit or Cursor with a Supabase backend, and small agencies that build such apps for local clients. They pay $149-$499 per incident plus $29/month monitoring.
problem: On Sept 25, 2026 UpGuard reported about 16,000 Supabase databases publicly exposing names, home addresses, phone numbers, passwords, auth tokens, private conversations and license plate records. AI coding tools write SQL migrations where Row-Level Security defaults to off, and founders never turn it on. An earlier flaw, CVE-2025-48757, exposed 170+ Lovable apps. Owners do not know how to fix it without breaking the app, whether anyone actually accessed the data, or whether they now have a legal duty to notify users and regulators.
solution: Not another scanner, since ShipSafe and VibeAppScanner already exist. This is a response desk. (1) The owner authorizes a read-only check on their own project. (2) The tool generates and tests an RLS policy pull request for common patterns (owner-only rows, public read and owner write, storage buckets) that does not break the app. (3) It reviews available Supabase API and Postgres logs to estimate whether anonymous-key access from unknown sources occurred. (4) A partner privacy attorney's state-by-state and GDPR decision tree produces a notification-or-not memo. (5) It drafts user notices and an evidence packet for the owner's cyber insurer. Continuous monitoring is upsell.
why_now: The UpGuard disclosure is three days old, and Cursor AI is the fastest-growing Glimpse trend of 2026 (+2,213%), with Cyber Insurance up 763% on Exploding Topics. Mass disclosures of this kind will keep recurring as more founders ship AI-built apps. Legal clocks (GDPR 72 hours, state laws with 30-60 day windows) create urgency at exactly the moment the owner learns of the exposure.
revenue_model: $149 lockdown-only tier, $499 lockdown plus log review plus notification memo and letters, $29/month continuous monitoring, and $99/client wholesale packages for agencies. Later: referral fees from cyber insurers and privacy counsel.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone sells detection. Nobody sells the 'now what', and the mission-critical question for an owner is legal, not technical. The trigger is public and fresh: UpGuard found ~16,000 exposed Supabase databases, the root cause is that AI-written migrations leave RLS off, and Supabase's CISO says security 'ultimately remains a shared responsibility' (https://startupfortune.com/upguard-found-16000-supabase-databases-leaking-user-data-to-the-open-web/). CVE-2025-48757 previously exposed 170+ Lovable apps, and the common failure is founders who cannot debug RLS (https://www.superblocks.com/blog/lovable-vulnerabilities). The scanner market already exists (https://vibeappscanner.com/lovable-security), which means paid demand is proven while the response step remains unowned. Cursor AI's +2,213% growth is the #1 item at https://meetglimpse.com/trends/.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the read-only exposure checker that owners run on their own project, plus an RLS policy generator for the five most common patterns. Days 8-15: co-author a 'Supabase RLS was off, what now? (24-hour plan)' guide with a privacy attorney and publish it for SEO and Reddit (r/lovable, r/supabase, Indie Hackers). Days 16-30: sell 20 lockdown fixes at $149-$199 and sign 2 small agencies at wholesale rates. Skip scanning anyone's databases without their authorization.

title: Drought-to-Curtailment Forecasts for Hydro-Powered Compute
one_liner: A subscription index that forecasts 30-180 day power-curtailment risk for bitcoin miners and AI data centers on hydro-dependent grids, built from rainfall, inflow and reservoir signals.
customer: Bitcoin mining hosts and data-center operators in hydro-heavy grids (East Africa, southern Africa, Central Asia, Paraguay, Pacific Northwest), plus their lenders, equipment financiers and insurers. Operators and lenders pay.
problem: Step one: Ethiopia cut power to miners by 75% during an El Nino drought, when reservoir inflows fell about 20% in a month. Miners use over a third of a grid that is 90% hydro. Step two: every hydro grid with growing crypto and AI load faces the same triage. Step three: hosts and lenders are financing sites on 'firm cheap green power' contracts with no drought-risk model.
solution: Combine satellite rainfall, soil moisture, snowpack, ENSO outlooks and satellite-measured reservoir levels into a probability of curtailed hours per site. Map it to each grid's known dispatch rules. Backtest against Ethiopia 2026 and the 2024 Kariba (Zambia/Zimbabwe) load-shedding. Deliver a weekly dashboard and a lender-diligence report.
why_now: El Nino drought is live, WMO calls this one of the driest years for the world's rivers in 35 years, and compute loads are chasing cheap hydro. Grids have now made compute-versus-water triage an explicit decision.
revenue_model: $2-10k/month per operator portfolio, $10-30k per lender or insurer diligence report, and later an index licensed for parametric cover.
non_obvious_insight: The risk being mispriced is hydrological, not political, and the party who needs the forecast is the compute host's lender, not the grid. A dry year is a correlated credit event across every hydro-powered site.
first_30_days: Build a public-data prototype for five reservoirs. Publish a free weekly brief aimed at miners and hosting firms. Backtest and publish the Ethiopia and Kariba case studies. Pitch three hosting firms and two mining lenders for paid pilots.

title: Mini Cat Bonds for Co-ops and Counties
one_liner: Cat bond capital is at record highs but deals under $50M are uneconomic. Make a $5-25M cat bond a 90-day, low-cost, template product for the sponsors the market ignores.
customer: Small public risk pools, rural electric cooperatives, counties, hospital systems and small regional insurers needing $5M-$50M of catastrophe protection.
problem: Cat bond issuance is a record $18.9B year to date with $65.6B outstanding, yet legal, modeling, rating and SPV costs of $1M-plus put small deals out of reach. Small sponsors stay in the traditional market or go bare, while primary property markets stay hard.
solution: A standardized private cat bond or collateralized reinsurance template: pre-approved documents, standard parametric triggers with an independent calculation agent, treasury-fund collateral with transparent accounting, and a target all-in cost under $150k with issuance in about 90 days. Sell the notes to ILS funds seeking diversification.
why_now: Record traditional and ILS capital, softening through 2027 (Jefferies), and mature tokenized and money-market collateral (Goldman put a $100B Treasury fund into crypto plumbing, CoinDesk 2026-09-28). ILS investors want diversification beyond Florida wind.
revenue_model: 1.5-3% of limit as a structuring fee, plus annual administration and calculation-agent fees.
non_obvious_insight: Softening means capital wants to deploy, so the binding constraint is deal cost per dollar of limit. That is a documentation and operations problem, not a risk-appetite problem.
first_30_days: Retain an offshore law firm and a calculation agent. Find two state pooling associations with wildfire or hail exposure, get indications of interest from two ILS funds, and produce a reusable term-sheet template. Charge a structuring retainer to fund first-deal work.

title: Disaster-Pause Rider for Small-Business Loans
one_liner: A parametric portfolio rider that lets CDFIs and credit unions automatically pause small-business and farm loan payments after a disaster, with the lender made whole by a pre-funded payout.
customer: Community lenders (CDFIs, credit unions, farm-credit and small-bank lenders) with $50-$500M loan books in disaster-exposed counties. The end beneficiaries are their small-business and consumer borrowers.
problem: After a hurricane, flood or fire, borrowers need a payment holiday, but lenders cannot afford to grant them automatically because the missed cash flow strains liquidity and reserves. Borrowers must plead, forbearance takes weeks of staff time, and many quietly default. CDFI funding is already fragile, so lenders hold back.
solution: A portfolio-level parametric policy keyed to county-level disaster declarations plus hazard footprints (wind swaths, flood extent, fire perimeters). It pays the lender the scheduled payments of borrowers in the footprint for 90-180 days. The loan documents carry a pre-approved 'automatic pause' clause, so borrowers never buy insurance. The lender markets 'storm-proof loans' and adds a rate rider of about 10-25 bps to pay for it. A software pause engine flags affected loans and sends notices.
why_now: Repeated large disasters and ongoing debate over shrinking or slowing federal disaster aid make private, fast liquidity more attractive. Federal support for CDFIs has been unsettled, so lenders want to protect portfolios. Parametric capacity is abundant and hazard-footprint data (NOAA swaths, flood extents) is public and precise.
revenue_model: MGA/brokerage fee of 15-20% on premium (roughly 25-60 bps of covered balance per year), plus a SaaS fee of $1,000-$5,000 per month for the pause-and-notice engine. Later, reinsurance placement and a data product on borrower resilience.
non_obvious_insight: After a disaster the scarce resource is lender liquidity, not rebuilding capital. A forbearance favor becomes a contractual right that costs the lender one clause, and distribution is the loan itself, so no borrower ever has to shop for or understand insurance.
first_30_days: Approach three Gulf Coast, Carolinas or California CDFIs and credit unions through CDFI trade networks. Write a one-page term sheet, price it from historical hazard footprints, and pilot on newly originated loans in one county. Pair with an MGA and a reinsurer, and target one signed letter of intent within 60 days.

title: Genki Tap: Konbini Clerks as Paid Elder Watchers
one_liner: Pay convenience-store staff to log a three-second 'seen and how they seemed' note on enrolled elderly regulars, and alert family and local support centers when someone goes quiet or drifts.
customer: Adult children living outside Osaka with a widowed or single parent in the city, at about ¥1,480 a month. Later customers are municipal community support centers (chiiki hokatsu shien centers) paying per enrolled senior, and eventually banks, trust banks and insurers that need early cognitive-decline and fraud signals.
problem: In 2025, 76,941 people died alone at home in Japan, 58,919 of them aged 65 or older. The Cabinet Office estimates about 22,222 were found after 8 or more days. Municipalities have signed 'elder-watching network' MOUs with konbini, post offices and newspaper carriers, but they are unpaid goodwill. The clerk notices, if that clerk happens to be on shift and cares, and the observation never becomes structured data. Owners know who has not come in for three days. We notice the customer buying the same item twice in a day, paying slowly with coins, forgetting the wallet, or getting confused at self-checkout. None of it reaches the family or the ward.
solution: The senior gets a keychain NFC tag or simply says a name. At the register, staff tap a ¥1,500 reader or a tablet and press one of three buttons: fine, a bit off, worried. If an enrolled senior is not seen for 48-72 hours, the system messages the family and a designated neighbor, then the local support center. The family gets a weekly digest such as 'came Mon, Wed, Thu; usual purchases; once forgot wallet'. The store earns ¥300-500 per enrolled senior per month, so the attention is paid for and survives shift changes. Consent is opt-in, data is minimal, and the escalation path runs through licensed care managers.
why_now: The National Police Agency now publishes annual solitary-death counts, and the 2025 figures show no decline. Municipalities are legally responsible for loneliness and isolation measures under the 2024 loneliness law. Post-2024 summer heat deaths at home have raised demand from families. Cashless and prepaid-card fraud aimed at seniors is also rising, so a clerk who already knows the customer is the best front-line filter.
revenue_model: Family subscription of ¥1,480 a month, of which ¥300-500 goes to the store. Municipal or support-center contracts pay per enrolled senior. Later, anonymized cognitive-drift signals feed paid programs from banks, trust companies and insurers concerned about dementia-related frozen assets and fraud.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource in elder monitoring is not sensors or AI, it is a trusted human who sees the person daily and is already 24/7 in the neighborhood. Municipal networks fail because the clerk's attention is unpaid and unstructured. A ¥300 payment plus a three-button interface turns free goodwill into reliable, recurring, auditable data. The store that sees the drift first is the konbini, not the clinic.
first_30_days: Enroll 8-10 owners in Ikuno, Nishinari, Higashinari and Abeno wards, starting with my own three stores. Use a LINE OA for families and cheap NFC readers or a phone app for staff. Identify 30 regulars whose adult children live in Tokyo, Nagoya or Fukuoka and pitch them by phone; aim for 50 paying families at ¥1,480. Sign an MOU with one community support center as the escalation partner. Log every alert and outcome so the pilot produces evidence for a municipal contract.

title: Immune-Training Forest-Floor Yards for Daycares
one_liner: A certified installation and refill service that replaces sterile daycare yards with vetted forest floor and sod to diversify children's skin and gut microbiota.
customer: Private daycare chains, preschool operators, nature-based preschools and municipal early-childhood departments in cities, especially ones competing on parent trust and outdoor programming.
problem: Allergies, asthma and immune disorders are rising in urban kids, who spend 8+ hours a day in daycare yards of plastic, gravel and rubber mulch with almost no microbial diversity. Parents worry, but the options are vague 'nature play' features with no evidence of health impact.
solution: Biodiversity kits based on the Finnish protocol: about 100 m2 of pathogen-screened forest floor litter and 200 m2 of sod, planter boxes and simple play rules, sourced from vetted local woodland. We add a seasonal refill and an optional microbiome swab study, all under a 'Biodiversity Certified' badge that daycares can show to parents.
why_now: There is direct peer-reviewed evidence. In a study of 10 Finnish daycares with 75 children aged 3-5, adding forest floor and sod for 28 days changed skin and gut microbiota and immune markers (Roslund et al., Science Advances, 2020), and a 2021 follow-up on long-term effects was published. Parents are more microbiome-aware, and cities are funding cooling and greening of schoolyards.
revenue_model: One-time install of roughly $6-15k per yard plus an annual refill subscription of roughly $1-2k per year, since the biology decays and litter needs replacing. Licensing of the certification badge to chains, and public-tender revenue from cities.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody can patent dirt, so the moat is safe sourcing, pathogen testing and certification, and the recurring consumable makes it a regional supply chain of local ecological material. Selling 'immune infrastructure' to childcare works because the buyer's real problem is parent trust, and a visible, evidence-backed feature beats a marketing claim.
first_30_days: Contact 10 forest schools and one small chain. Build a 30 m2 pilot with a local soil scientist and a university microbiologist for about $1.5k. Set up a baseline and follow-up swab pilot and sell the first three paid yards to chains that want a differentiator.

title: Revocation List for Leaked ID Documents
one_liner: A neutral, hashed registry of compromised license and passport records that every verifier can check, forcing step-up on IDs from the Nexus/IDScan.net dump.
customer: IDV and KYC vendors, marketplaces, gig platforms, neobanks, telecom and car-rental retail, and lenders, buying an API.
problem: On Aug 31 2026 the Nexus market began selling 153M+ US and Canadian driver's licenses, each with six images including infrared and ultraviolet scans. Researchers call stored ID images 'permanent fraud tools'. Verifiers cannot tell a fresh scan from a leaked record, and issuers will not revoke tens of millions of licenses.
solution: Ingest breach corpora only through controlled, lawful channels (researcher and law-enforcement partners, hash-only contributions). Compute privacy-preserving fingerprints (salted hashes of document number, state and DOB combinations, and perceptual hashes of portraits). Expose an API answering 'has this document instance been seen compromised?' with a risk tier and recommended step-up (mobile ID, bank-account link, in-person). Add hash-prefix consumer lookup and DMV reissue guidance.
why_now: The Nexus dump is the biggest leak of ID scans and follows 2025 leaks of ID photos from age-verification and support systems (e.g., Discord's vendor). Document-image KYC now needs a compensating signal, and verifiers have none.
revenue_model: $0.01-0.05 per check or $2-20K per month subscriptions, with consumer-alert partnerships through banks.
non_obvious_insight: Public-key infrastructure solved 'a trusted key was stolen' with revocation lists, not by preventing theft. Issuers will not revoke documents, but verifiers can pool what they know. The leak itself is the data source, and the value comes from the shared list.
first_30_days: Partner with 2-3 breach researchers and one small IDV vendor. Build the hashing pipeline and API, and clear the design with privacy counsel. Give it free to 10 verifiers, then convert by usage.

title: Warranty-Linked Installer Certification for African Solar Batteries
one_liner: Battery and inverter brands pay per certified installer and per registered installation, and every certification requires geotagged commissioning proof, which builds an installed-base registry that lenders and insurers cannot otherwise get.
customer: Battery and inverter brands and their distributors in Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana (and Indian rooftop and backup-power distributors), paying about $8-15 per registered install plus certification event fees. Asset lenders and insurers pay later for registry data. Installers pay $15-25 for the badge.
problem: Africa has imported more battery dollars than panel dollars from China since 2024, and 75% of solar growth is distributed. Ember estimates its numbers are 2x the official statistics, and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data. Bad installs (loose lugs, undersized cable, misconfigured battery communications) drive warranty costs and fires. Brands cannot tell who installed what and where. Lenders and insurers cannot price the risk.
solution: A 2-day practical certification in a rented workshop with real inverters, batteries and torque tests, run by senior local installers. After certification, every job requires a geotagged photo checklist and serial scans through a WhatsApp or lightweight app flow, and the brand's warranty desk validates instantly. In return installers get faster claims, brand lead flow and pricing power. Trainees come from underemployed electrical-engineering graduates and, reportedly, technicians returning from Gulf jobs.
why_now: Africa is installing about 17 GW in 2026 (+45% year on year), with batteries now the larger import dollar. The Hormuz-linked energy shock and diesel costs push more households and shops toward backup power. India's induction-cooktop rush (reported 20-25x demand) is stressing home wiring and backup systems. Official statistics cannot see any of it, so private registries have unusual value.
revenue_model: $8-15 per registered install from the brand, $1-3k per certification event, and $15-25 badge fees from installers. Lenders and insurers pay $20-60k a year for registry access, or per-lookup fees.
non_obvious_insight: The certification is the data-collection mechanism. Nobody can sell a registry to a lender directly, but every installer will sign up for a badge that speeds warranty claims, and the registry is exhaust from that. It fixes the exact blind spot Ember describes, and the payer at the start is the brand with a warranty bill, not the trainee.
first_30_days: Pick Lagos or Nairobi. Sign one distributor of a top-five battery brand as the pilot payer, using its own warranty-claim cost as the case. Rent a workshop and certify 30-40 installers on day one, with the distributor covering $20 per head. Use WhatsApp plus a form tool with serial-number OCR and no custom code. Target 300 registered installs in 90 days and show the brand the change in its claim rate.

title: Contrast Capture: Recovering Iodine From Post-Scan Urine
one_liner: Capture iodinated and gadolinium contrast agents from patients' urine at CT and MRI centers, funded by the drug makers who now owe EU wastewater EPR fees, and recover the iodine and gadolinium.
customer: Contrast-media producers and their EPR schemes (the payer), imaging centers and hospital radiology departments (the host), and water utilities. Start in the Netherlands, Germany, the Nordics and Switzerland.
problem: Contrast agents are excreted almost entirely unchanged within about a day, pass through conventional wastewater treatment, and show up in rivers and drinking water (anthropogenic gadolinium anomalies are documented near large cities). The recast EU Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive now requires pharma and cosmetics producers to fund at least 80% of quaternary treatment costs. Treating a whole city's effluent for one class of molecule is expensive and contrast agents are very persistent. Meanwhile iodine (tens of grams per contrast CT) and the rare earth gadolinium are supply-concentrated materials being flushed away.
solution: At-source capture in radiology: single-use polymer-lined urine bags or urine-diverting toilets in the imaging suite, handed out at check-out with a prepaid courier or bin for the first voids. A central facility recovers iodine and gadolinium by ion exchange and crystallization and returns them to producers as recycled input. The product sold to producers is 'verified kilograms of contrast removed from the water cycle', a metric their EPR schemes can count against fees. Hospitals get a 'green radiology' certification.
why_now: The recast UWWTD (Directive 2024/3019) is in force and producers are beginning to work out how to meet the 80% cost share, so source-control measures are being sought now. Rare-earth and critical-materials recovery is politically fashionable, giving hospitals and funders a second reason to say yes.
revenue_model: Per-patient capture fee paid by producers or their EPR fund (a few euros per scan), plus sale of recovered iodine and gadolinium (worth roughly $1-3 of iodine per contrast CT, so it supplements rather than carries the business), plus utility co-funding contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The materials are worth pennies to a few dollars per patient; the real revenue is the avoided cost of tertiary and quaternary treatment plants, and the party who owes it is not the hospital but the drug companies. A waste business with a pharma-industry payer.
first_30_days: Sign letters of intent with two imaging centers and one water utility in the Netherlands or Germany. Run a 200-patient pilot with off-the-shelf urine bags and a university lab to measure capture rates and patient compliance. Present the data to the producers' trade body and to the EPR scheme designers as a candidate 'innovative measure' needing pilot funding.

title: Water Due Diligence for Senior Housing Deals
one_liner: A 'Phase I for water' that grades a senior living property or CCRC bond on supply security, drought exposure, contamination compliance and in-building Legionella risk before lenders and buyers commit.
customer: HUD-232 and bridge lenders, senior-housing acquirers and Sunbelt developers, CCRC bond underwriters and muni credit analysts, and insurers. Pricing is $4-12k per deal report and $25-60k a year for portfolio subscriptions.
problem: Senior housing occupancy is 90.1%, the highest since 2007, and construction is the lowest since 2012 with a roughly $275B shortfall. New development will restart in Sunbelt states where Colorado River cuts (2027+), groundwater rules, PFAS and lead compliance, and drought restrictions bite. The asset class is uniquely exposed: 24/7 occupancy, heavy laundry, kitchens and cooling towers, frail residents you cannot evacuate, and Legionella that kills mostly older adults. CCRC bonds promise care for life on 30-year horizons, yet a standard environmental Phase I says nothing about water security.
solution: A standard report covering legally deliverable supply, the provider's source portfolio (river, groundwater, reuse), moratorium and curtailment history, a five-year rate outlook, PFAS, lead and nitrate compliance of the serving utility, and an in-building water-management-plan audit (Legionella per CMS and ASHRAE 188, cooling towers). It also covers drought-restriction impacts on operations and NOI sensitivity to a 30% water-cost spike. Output is a letter grade plus capex and insurance recommendations, with a portfolio dashboard for bond analysts.
why_now: Record occupancy and accelerating investment mean a wave of acquisitions and new starts is coming. The Colorado River decision framework landed in Aug 2026, PFAS monitoring starts in 2027, and Texas's data-center water crackdown showed water is now an explicit siting factor.
revenue_model: Per-report fees of $4-12k, annual subscriptions of $25-60k for bond funds and lender credit desks, and remediation referral fees from the sensor and water-treatment vendors that fix the flagged items.
non_obvious_insight: For senior housing, water risk is life-safety, not just cost. Residents cannot leave and the pathogens are lethal, so it should be underwritten like fire risk, yet nobody sells the underwriting standard. The first credible grade becomes the lender checklist item.
first_30_days: Publish a free water-risk map of the 60 largest CCRC and senior-housing bond issuers in Colorado River, Texas and Florida stress zones. Email it to 30 muni analysts and 10 HUD lenders, and offer three discounted deal reports at $3k.

title: Paid Exit Capture: Layoffs Become Agent Evals
one_liner: Pay departing employees a completion bonus to turn their tacit exception-handling know-how into the eval sets and edge-case playbooks the employer's AI agents need, before that knowledge walks out.
customer: Head of AI, COO or CHRO at 1,000-20,000-person companies running AI-justified headcount cuts in ops-heavy functions (claims, support, finance ops, procurement), plus PE operating partners doing portfolio-wide cuts.
problem: Companies cut the people who know the long tail, then find their agents fail on it. Reversals are now reported (Klarna rehiring humans in 2025, Commonwealth Bank of Australia reversing 45 cuts, CNBC's Jul 2026 'regret' headline). Exit interviews are HR theatre, and angry leavers have no reason to document anything.
solution: A 2-3 week 'capture sprint' inside the notice or severance window. A consented, paid interview agent plus a domain reviewer walks each person through their 50 hardest cases. Output is a graded eval set (inputs, gold decisions, rubrics, 'when I'd escalate') and a playbook the employer owns. Workers get a bonus scaled to eval quality (measured by held-out agent accuracy), a signed contribution credential and optionally a recall or contract-rights clause.
why_now: AI was the top-cited layoff reason in Challenger data for five straight months through Jul 2026, and enterprise agent rollouts are now bottlenecked by evals and edge cases rather than by models. Reversal stories are giving CFOs a fresh fear. Interview agents are cheap enough to run the sprints at scale.
revenue_model: $15-40k fixed fee per role-cluster capture sprint (roughly $1.5-4k per captured employee after bonuses), plus an annual eval-refresh retainer once the agent is live.
non_obvious_insight: To the employer a laid-off worker is a depreciating liability, but for the agent rollout they are the only source of ground truth on the long tail. You can only get it by paying, and paying on eval quality fixes the incentive. The data is worth far more than the severance delta.
first_30_days: Use public WARN filings to list 40 companies mid-layoff and pitch 15 HR/AI leads a free 5-person pilot at cost. Have an employment lawyer draft the consent, IP-assignment and NDA carve-out template. Deliver one eval set and show before/after agent accuracy as the case study.

title: Robot Pack-Opening with Chain-of-Custody
one_liner: A neutral facility and machine that opens sealed trading-card packs on camera without human hands, sorts hits and ships them, so buyers can trust a break.
customer: Live-stream breakers and repack sellers, game stores running mail-in breaks, and buyers who pay for the 'bot-opened' badge.
problem: Fraud in streamed breaks includes resealed packs with hits removed, counterfeits and non-delivery. Whatnot did about $8B in 2025 and is under litigation, X-ray pack scanning is sold to collectors, and breakers spend heavy labor opening thousands of packs.
solution: A semi-automated cell (slitter, camera, card ID, sleeving) with serial-logged tamper-evident intake seals, a public feed with an audit trail, and a badge. Start as a neutral facility with humans in the loop, opening product breakers ship in, then lease the machine to large breakers.
why_now: Vision-language robot control matured in 2025-26. Litigation and fraud make trust monetizable, and the 2026 robbery wave favors a secured central facility over home streaming setups.
revenue_model: $0.40-1.00 per pack opened, per-hit shipping fees, badge subscriptions and machine leasing.
non_obvious_insight: Trust in breaks is a chain-of-custody problem, not a reputation problem. A machine has no motive to skim hits. Labor arbitrage pays for the machine while trust earns the price premium.
first_30_days: Rent a small secure space and run hands-off, sealed-bag-intake openings for 5 breakers with two part-timers and a phone rig. Charge per pack and prototype the cutter with an off-the-shelf arm.

title: Heatwave Demand Signals for Cool-Climate Hotels
one_liner: A revenue-management add-on that turns heatwave forecasts in origin cities into rate floors, minimum stays and direct-booking campaigns for hotels in cool refuge regions, days before the booking surge arrives.
customer: Independent hotels and guesthouses (20-150 rooms) and regional tourism boards in cool refuge regions: Scottish Highlands, Norwegian fjords, Galicia/Asturias/Cantabria, Baltic coast, Slovenian Alps, Irish west coast; in the US, the Oregon/Washington coast, Maine and Michigan's Upper Peninsula.
problem: Demand for cool regions surges within days of heat events in origin markets (London, Paris, Madrid, Milan, Chicago), but revenue managers set rates weekly from pace reports and holiday calendars. Booking lead times are shrinking (about 33 days versus 37.5). OTAs capture the last-minute surge at their own price, while 51% of European hotels already suspect OTAs of selling below loaded rates. Hotels underprice, sell out cheaply and lose direct-booking margin.
solution: Ingest open ensemble forecasts for roughly 150 origin metros. Calibrate lag and elasticity per hotel from its own booking curve (read-only PMS/channel-manager connection). Send a daily WhatsApp or email alert such as 'Heat dome over Madrid Thu-Sun; expect searches for Asturias to jump from Wednesday; raise floor 15%, add a 2-night minimum, push the direct offer to your Madrid and Barcelona email list.' Optionally trigger geo-targeted direct-booking ads and pre-approved regional DMO 'Cool Escape' co-op campaigns.
why_now: Summer 2026 produced rerouted, last-minute, value-driven travel (Europe ADR +4-6%, shorter lead times). Google AI Overviews now show hotel prices and reportedly cut metasearch click-through 31% in tests, so hotels must capture surges through their own channels. Booking's merchant model is eroding rate control. 'Coolcation' travel is mainstream enough that destinations market it openly.
revenue_model: $79-199 per month per property, an optional performance fee of 3% of incremental direct revenue, and DMO campaign licenses of $15-40K per season.
non_obvious_insight: Heat in the origin market is a public leading indicator that hotel systems are blind to, because they were built around event and holiday calendars. The edge is a 72-hour timing arbitrage against OTAs. It doubles as a dispersal tool, steering demand from saturated Mediterranean hotspots to under-visited regions that tourism boards are eager to promote.
first_30_days: Backtest July-August 2026 with 5 hotels' booking curves under NDA and quantify money left on the table during the heat dome. Publish the case study. Ship v0 as a Google Sheet plus a weather API plus WhatsApp alerts. Sell two regional DMO pilots (Galicia, Scottish Highlands) for a triggered spring campaign.

title: Harvest Inns: Motel Wings as Farm Crew Housing
one_liner: A hospitality-grade operator that master-leases wings of underused rural motels and sublets compliant beds, meals and transport to growers who cannot house H-2A crews.
customer: Fruit and vegetable growers and grower associations using H-2A labor in Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Washington and Florida. The supply side is independent rural motels and extended-stay properties.
problem: Housing is the binding constraint on legally staffing harvests. Farm crews shrank after the immigration crackdown (up to 30% of strawberry and almond crews lost in Q1 2026), grapes, blueberries and peaches rotted unpicked in 2025, and H-2A jobs are heading toward 500K. Growers do not want to run hotels, and motel owners do not want H-2A paperwork while their occupancy stays weak in a K-shaped market.
solution: Master-lease 20-40 room wings for 10-16 weeks. Run the compliance layer: DOL public-accommodation rules (50 sq ft per person, 36-inch bed spacing, cooking and laundry ratios, direct payment by the employer to housing management), pre-built state workforce agency inspection files, linens and cleaning, catered or kitchenette meals and van shuttles. Software rebooks the same crews' beds in the next county as harvest calendars move, like a hotel chain whose guests are harvest crews. Inspection-first and worker-first standards are the moat.
why_now: DOL rules explicitly allow hotels and motels as H-2A housing, with local health codes applying first. The October 2025 wage-rule change and H-2A growth mean more growers are entering a system they have never staffed. Late crews and unpicked fields are now widely reported, and lower-tier hotels are under pressure while luxury leads.
revenue_model: Growers pay roughly $22-$35 per bed-night all-in (assumption to validate), of which motels get about $12-$20. Operator margin of 20-30% plus meal and transport upsells, sold as season contracts through grower associations.
non_obvious_insight: The idle asset already exists in every farm county, and the missing party is a specialist workforce-lodging operator, the ag version of oil-field man camps, who will absorb compliance risk. Motel owners value a guaranteed off-OTA base load more than a higher rate.
first_30_days: Pick one cluster such as south Georgia blueberries and peaches or Michigan cherries. Sign 3 motels for wings of 20-40 rooms, map the state inspection process with the workforce agency, and pre-sell 2 growers before March for the spring 2027 harvest season.

title: Contingency Appeals for Denied Pet Insurance Claims
one_liner: Insurers rely on paperwork friction to keep denials uncontested; LLMs that assemble records and policy language make appeals cheap enough to work for a success fee.
customer: Pet owners with denied or reduced claims of roughly $1,500-$15,000 (pre-existing, bilateral, hereditary or 'curable' exclusion disputes), reached through owner communities and vet front desks.
problem: Premiums rose about 19.7% in 2025 while insured animals grew 9%, so owners are angry and paying more for coverage that may not pay. An appeal requires pulling every prior clinic's records, reading policy definitions and getting a vet statement. Most owners give up.
solution: Owner uploads the denial letter and policy. We automate records requests to past clinics, read records against the policy's definitions and the state's pet-insurance rules, draft the appeal with a contracted DVM's signed medical statement, file it, and escalate to the state insurance department if needed. Fee is 15-25% of recovered dollars, nothing upfront.
why_now: As of early 2026, 28 states had adopted or introduced versions of the NAIC Pet Insurance Model Act, which creates disclosure and pre-existing-condition hooks and formal complaint routes. LLMs can now read messy multi-clinic records cheaply. Premium hikes are driving search intent and anger.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 15-25% of recovered claims. Second product: anonymized denial-pattern intelligence sold to regulators, clinics and insurers who want fewer disputes.
non_obvious_insight: Denial rates are sustained by the cost of contesting, not by the merits. That cost was human labor. Once evidence assembly is near-free, the spread between 'denied' and 'overturned when documented' becomes a business, and it produces the best dataset on how insurers actually deny.
first_30_days: Post 'no win, no fee appeals' in pet-owner communities and take 30 cases. Contract one vet to sign statements at $75-150 each. Track overturn rate; kill criterion is under 20%. Check state public-adjuster and unauthorized-practice rules before charging a contingency fee.

title: Blind Validation Enclaves for Clinical AI
one_liner: Confidential-computing sandboxes where a hospital's private patient data and a vendor's private model meet, and only a signed performance report leaves.
customer: Health-system AI governance committees and health-AI vendors (imaging, ambient scribes, risk models), plus payers and insurers of AI performance guarantees.
problem: Hospitals cannot validate vendor claims on their own patients because PHI cannot leave and vendors will not ship weights. Published metrics rarely transfer to local populations. The Joint Commission and the Coalition for Health AI issued responsible-AI guidance in Sept 2025 and planned voluntary certification, so buyers now need evidence.
solution: A managed enclave (confidential VMs and GPUs) deployed in the hospital's own cloud tenant. The vendor's container runs against local retrospective data. Attestation proves that the evaluation code was unmodified and nothing was exfiltrated. The output is a signed report on subgroup performance, calibration and drift, repeated quarterly as post-deployment monitoring.
why_now: Confidential GPUs became generally available on major clouds in 2025, health systems adopted ambient scribes and imaging AI at scale, and Joint Commission and CHAI guidance created a demand for third-party assurance. The vendor-paid validation model is visibly conflicted.
revenue_model: $25-75k per validation (split between hospital and vendor), $10k per quarter monitoring, and payer or insurer programmes.
non_obvious_insight: Neither party trusts the other with its crown jewel, and the usual referee (the vendor) is conflicted. A machine that both sides can cryptographically verify replaces the trusted third party, so the product is the attestation as much as the test.
first_30_days: Partner with one academic medical centre's informatics team and two imaging or scribe vendors for a single use-case pilot. Use an existing confidential-computing offering rather than building infrastructure.

title: Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders
one_liner: Turn the vet's preg-check clipboard into a borrower-consented, third-party-verified herd inventory that banks can lend against.
customer: Community banks, Farm Credit associations and ag lenders with cattle loan books (they require it or pay per report, usually passed through to the borrower). Secondary payer is the cow-calf or heifer-development operator who wants bigger operating lines or bred-heifer financing on better terms.
problem: Cattle collateral has no VIN. Lenders verify with drive-by counts and borrower-supplied spreadsheets, and prosecutors in 2026 alleged a roughly $9.4M fraud that included a loan of $2.8M against 850 head. Farm loan delinquencies are rising while bred cows trade around $3,000+ per head, so a 500-cow borrower is $1.5M+ of collateral that nobody independent has counted.
solution: A 'Verified Herd Report' generated at the working day the vet is already doing. The vet or tech logs every head with an EID or visual tag scan (a $500 handheld reader plus a phone app), age class, pregnancy status and stage, and location. The vet e-signs and the borrower approves sharing with one tap. The lender gets a portal with timestamped, geotagged counts and year-over-year flags (head count down, pregnancy rate down, tags not matching last year). A second light pass happens at weaning. The vet earns a per-head fee for data they already write down and throw in the truck door pocket.
why_now: Federal EID ear tags became mandatory for many interstate cattle movements in Nov 2024, so per-head digital ID is now normal and cheap. Herd rebuilding at record cattle prices is being financed with debt, lenders entered 2026 carrying operating losses from 2023-2025 (rising delinquencies and restructures), and a fresh cattle-collateral fraud case is making ag loan committees ask for verification. Fall preg-check season is running right now (Sept-Nov).
revenue_model: $2-3 per head per verification, split roughly 50/50 with the vet practice, charged to the borrower or the lender as a loan condition. Add a portfolio dashboard for lenders at $500-2,000 per month once an institution has 100+ verified borrowers. Later, sell the verified inventory and pregnancy data to lenders as an underwriting input (advance rates on verified bred heifers).
non_obvious_insight: The vet is the only independent professional who physically handles every animal in the herd once or twice a year. They count, tag-check and pregnancy-check every cow, and that data dies on a clipboard. Vets refuse to police clients, but they will happily attest to what they handled when the borrower initiates the request, so the conflict-of-interest problem disappears. Honest borrowers are the real buyers: verified bred females can justify higher advance rates, and that cheap capital funds the fee many times over.
first_30_days: Preg-check season is live, so sign up 3 rural practices that each do several thousand head of fall preg-checks. Pitch 3-4 community-bank ag lenders (target the one who has been burned by a herd count before; work through state bankers' association ag committees). Run a pilot on about 10 willing borrowers with a form-based app and a PDF report, charging $2/head. Gather a before and after on what the lender learned that the drive-by inspection missed, then use that to sell the annual program.

title: Notarized Sky: Satellite Image Authenticity Desk
one_liner: A verification desk that tells insurers, traders and newsrooms whether a 'satellite photo' is real, by corroborating it against independent archives and issuing a signed chain-of-custody attestation.
customer: Marine war-risk and political-violence underwriters and brokers in the London market, commodity and energy trading desks, and verification desks at wire services and OSINT outlets. Second wave: parametric insurers whose triggers depend on Earth-observation data, and arbitration or sanctions law firms.
problem: Generative tools can now fabricate or subtly edit overhead imagery, and viral 'satellite photos' of strikes, burning tankers or troop moves circulate in every conflict, moving prices and claims. Buyers assume satellites are physics-grade truth, but the last mile is a JPEG on social media and vendors sell pixels, not provenance. With the Strait of Hormuz reportedly closed since March 2026, war-risk claims and rumor-driven price moves are large.
solution: (1) Rapid 'witness triangulation': check the claimed place and time against open archives (Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2, Landsat) and quick commercial archive pulls (optical and SAR), plus sun-angle and shadow geometry, cloud and terrain consistency, and vessel positions versus AIS and RF logs. (2) Forensics for synthetic or edited artifacts and C2PA/EXIF provenance. (3) A signed, hash-timestamped corroboration report usable in claims files and disputes. (4) For imagery buyers, verify delivered files against provider manifests.
why_now: Hormuz disruption created a wave of unverifiable incident claims. EU AI Act Article 50(2) synthetic-content marking applies from 2 Dec 2026 for systems already on the market, raising attention on provenance. Commodity EO and SAR are cheap and frequent (Planet targets up to 10 revisits a day), but no cross-vendor 'signed pixels' standard exists.
revenue_model: $2.5-8K per rapid verification report (24-hour SLA) and $8-20K per month retainers for underwriters and desks. Later, metered API access for parametric insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Detection accuracy is not the product; corroboration is. Government-held archives cannot be retroactively edited by an attacker, and SAR sees through cloud and is not something a text-to-image model can fake convincingly. A tiny team can be an independent witness cheaply. What buyers actually pay for is a defensible attestation, a SOC report for pixels, that survives a claims dispute.
first_30_days: Publish teardowns of 3 viral fake or misattributed satellite images from 2025-26 conflicts, each with reproducible multi-source refutations. Send them to 25 marine war-risk brokers and 15 newsroom verification desks. Sell 3 rapid-verification pilots at $2.5K each and convert one underwriter to a retainer.

title: Verified-Human Capture for Robot Training Data
one_liner: A trusted-capture layer that proves robot training video was really filmed by a real human doing a real task on a real sensor, sold to data vendors and to the labs that buy from them.
customer: Robot-data collection networks (the long tail beneath XDOF and Mecka) and the humanoid makers and robot-foundation-model labs that buy their hours of first-person footage.
problem: Physical-world data is the humanoid bottleneck, and vendors pay gig workers to film themselves making coffee or fixing cars. Pay-per-effort markets get swamped by slop: cURL killed its bug bounty in Jan 2026 over AI-generated reports. AI video makes fake demos trivial. Workers can replay clips, script them or run multiple accounts, and buyers cannot QC hours at scale. One contaminated batch can poison a training run. Vendors grading their own data is the referee-grading-itself problem.
solution: A capture app and a certified head- or chest-mount kit that signs raw video, IMU and depth with device-bound keys in a C2PA-compatible manifest. Physics-consistency checks compare video-derived camera motion to the IMU trace, which generated video fails. Unique-worker checks without stored biometrics (on-device liveness, payout-account binding). Random human audit sampling and per-clip QA scores. A batch-level 'Certified Real' certificate buyers can verify.
why_now: Mecka is near a $500M valuation and XDOF hit about $50M annualized revenue within three months of leaving stealth. C2PA hit critical mass (TikTok joined in Jul 2026). EU AI Act Article 50 has applied since Aug 2, 2026. Biometric proof-of-personhood is being banned in places (Thailand, Kenya, Philippines), and verifier breaches (Persona, IDScan) push toward on-device proof.
revenue_model: $0.30-$1.50 per verified hour, paid by vendors who pass it through. $20/mo certified-kit rental per collector. Enterprise audits for large data buyers, $5k-$25k per batch program.
non_obvious_insight: In content, human-made is a nicety. In robot data, physically real and human-performed is the entire product, and synthetic data is a far cheaper competitor. A certificate showing which hours are real is what lets vendors keep a price premium, so vendors will pay for it. The verifier gets a toll on the fastest-growing data category without competing with anyone.
first_30_days: Ship an open-source signed-capture app and a physics-consistency checker. Offer 5 small data vendors a free audit of one sample batch and show them the share of clips that fail. Convert 2 to paid pilots at $2k-$5k/mo. Ship a 'Certified Real' batch stamp and a public verification page.

title: Plumber Doorstep Network for Lead Line Access
one_liner: Sell water utilities and their engineering consultants a local-plumber network that verifies unknown service-line materials, converts homeowner access agreements and does the interior tie-ins on lead and galvanized line replacements.
customer: Municipal and regional water utilities (10k-200k connections) with a large 'unknown material' share in their lead service line inventory, and the engineering consultants running their inventories and replacement programs, funded by state revolving funds and Bipartisan Infrastructure Law money.
problem: Utilities must identify every unknown-material service line and replace lead and galvanized-requiring-replacement lines, including the private side, under the federal Lead and Copper Rule Improvements; several states (Michigan, New Jersey, Illinois) have their own mandates. The bottleneck is not excavation, it is access. Mailer response rates are low, homeowner self-identification is unreliable, and people do not want a stranger from Public Works in the basement. The utility's excavation contractor also usually refuses to touch interior plumbing, so the interior reconnection sits in limbo. EPA's own August 2026 access-tips document exists because this is where programs stall.
solution: A branded 'Local Plumber Verification' visit. A licensed plumber or apprentice from a local shop knocks on a scheduled visit, checks the pipe where it enters the house (scratch and magnet test, the wiped-joint bulge, meter connection, photo protocol) in about 10 minutes, and uploads a GIS-ready record to the inventory. They get the access agreement signed on the spot, note obstructions (finished basement, boxed-in pipe, shutoff condition) and pre-scope the interior tie-in. A second product is the interior tie-in and shutoff replacement, done by the same shops as a subcontract to the utility's excavation contractor, with a warranty on the house side.
why_now: The federal rule's ten-year replacement clock, the compliance dates approaching in 2027, EPA's freshly updated access guidance, and billions in SRF and BIL money that has to be spent all converge. Utilities are now measured on unknown-line reduction, and consultants are looking for boots on the ground. Even if federal deadlines are softened, the state laws and the fact that unknown lines still have to be identified keep the demand.
revenue_model: $60-120 per verified line, $150-300 per signed access agreement (both paid by utility or consultant per unit), and a 15-20% margin on interior tie-in subcontracts ($400-1,500 each). The shop keeps most of the field labor and pays the network for lead flow, tooling, quality control and the reporting workflow.
non_obvious_insight: Homeowners trust the truck with a local plumber's name on it far more than a city letter, and the plumber can read a lead line faster than any model can read a mailer. The reason programs stall is that homeowners fear that letting anyone in means they will be found to have a problem and get a bill, and that the utility contractor will leave their basement half-connected. A plumber solves both, and plumbers are the only people who already have a license, insurance and an interior-work warranty.
first_30_days: Skip direct municipal procurement at first and sell to a mid-size engineering consultant who already holds the utility's inventory contract and needs subcontractors. Pick two utilities with a high unknown share and low mailer response. Propose a paid pilot of 300 addresses at a fixed price per verification. Recruit 3 shops that want steady work for apprentices. Build the mobile form and photo protocol in a form tool that exports to the utility's inventory template.
